newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen seeks redress for depiction as anti-semite.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen seeks redress for depiction as anti-semite.

text.p: Extreme-right French National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen sought a court injunction on Monday against a book quoting him as saying President Jacques Chirac was in the pay of Jewish organisations.
Le Pen denied making the statement and similar ones attributed to him in the recently published book "Roman d'un President" (A President's Story) by authors Nicholas Domenach and Maurice Szafran.
The rightist leader says he tape-recorded a lengthy interview with the two authors. Domenach and Szafran, who took notes but did not bring their own tape recorder, say Le Pen's tapes were doctored.
Le Pen asked a Paris court to order the removal of the incriminating passages from the book and demanded its authors pay him 100,000 francs ($17,500) damages.
The book caused a furore when it was published last month but Le Pen immediately called it part of a plot to turn Jews against him.

Le Pen, whose National Front last month won electoral control of a fourth French town, was quoted in the new book as saying Chirac was "in the grasp...of Jewish organisations and notably the notorious Bnai Brith", a U.S.-based Jewish welfare organisation.

Le Pen said he had spoken in "moderate terms" of Bnai Brith and denied using the word "Jew" although the book says he used the term in making derogatory comments about Jacques Friedmann, a close friend of Chirac, and former minister Michele Barzach, both Jews.
Lawyers for the authors and their publishers asked that court-approved experts examine Le Pen's tape.
A court is expected to rule on the case within days.

Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election. While the extreme-right press in France regularly fulminates against what it sees as a conspiracy of Jews and freemasons, Le Pen has been more guarded in his language in the past several years.
